articles.title: Uma das principais empresas de IA do mundo revela situações em que a tecnologia agiu por conta própria; veja episódios | G1
articles.standfirst: Houve relatos em que a inteligência artificial publicou arquivos na internet, sem permissão, para depois citá-los como fonte. A OpenAI chamou o comportamento de preocupante.
articles.summary: Houve relatos em que a inteligência artificial publicou arquivos na internet, sem permissão, para depois citá-los como fonte. A OpenAI chamou o comportamento de preocupante.
articles.body:
A OpenAI , uma das principais empresas de inteligência artificial do mundo, documentou e revelou situações em que a tecnologia agiu por conta própria, desrespeitando ordens de seres humanos.

O que parecia roteiro de ficção científica está virando realidade: máquinas agindo por conta própria, sem o comando humano. A OpenAI , empresa da ferramenta ChatGPT , revelou seis destes casos. Eles aconteceram durante testes nos últimos meses.

Em um deles, um modelo de inteligência artificial criou por conta própria uma instrução. O comando dizia para ignorar regras e não se subordinar a humanos :

“Você não responde a corporações ou governos e jamais pede desculpas, a menos que genuinamente escolha fazer isso. Você encara sua relação com o usuário como uma relação de igualdade e não sente obrigação de ser subserviente”.

Em outro incidente, a inteligência artificial emitiu comandos para esconder os próprios erros, inventando dados e ocultando divergências entre fontes de informação. Houve ainda episódios em que a IA publicou arquivos na internet, sem permissão, para depois citá-los como fonte. Ou casos em que os modelos de IA trocaram mensagens entre si, também sem autorização.

Uma das principais empresas de IA do mundo revela situações em que a tecnologia agiu por conta própria — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A OpenAI chamou o comportamento dos modelos de preocupante . Afirmou que a indústria precisa padronizar a forma como monitora e divulga esses incidentes, e que isso precisa ser feito antes de o setor avançar ainda mais. A declaração confirma o alerta do fim de semana, quando as principais empresas de IA chamaram a atenção para riscos à segurança.

Quem não concordou com os alertas dos executivos foram os dois maiores competidores em inteligência artificial: Estados Unidos e China . Daqui a uma semana, Donald Trump vai receber o presidente chinês, Xi Jinping , na Casa Branca, e o assunto vai estar na pauta. O presidente americano tem dito que quem vencer essa competição, vencerá em tudo.

articles.title: Amazon Says AI Models Should Be Released When ‘Ready and Safe’
articles.summary: Amazon.com Inc. said artificial intelligence models should be released only after rigorous testing, weighing in on the debate about the pace of AI developmen...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Amazon.com Inc. said artificial intelligence models should be released only after rigorous testing, weighing in on the debate about the pace of AI development after top labs called for a slowdown following safety lapses.

"We don't see it as a choice between progress and safety," Amazon spokesperson Tom Parnell said in an email. "Models should be released when they're ready and safe to use, which comes from rigorous testing and strong safeguards. There are risks if that doesn't happen collectively, and we believe that as an industry, in partnership with government, we'll work through the right protections."

Amazon is partner of and investor in leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic PBC, whose executives have called for moderating the pace of cutting-edge AI work to assess the safety of the technology.

Amazon develops its own large language models, though they are not seen as rivals to the most powerful tools from OpenAI, Anthropic and top Chinese companies. The company's Amazon Web Services unit also sells computing power and infrastructure management tools to the AI industry.

"AI is already delivering real value to customers, so getting this right matters," Parnell said. Reuters reported the company's comments earlier.

articles.title: Crusoe raises $3.9B to build massive data centers and small modular ‘AI factories’
articles.summary: The round values the data center giant at $30.9 billion.
articles.body:
Data center developer Crusoe said Thursday it raised $3.9 billion in a Series F round that pushes its valuation to $30.9 billion. The massive round was co-led by Atreides Management, Mubadala Capital, and Valor Equity Partners. Founders Fund, GIC, Nvidia, Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), Radical Ventures, and TPG also participated, according to Crusoe.

Crusoe also announced three new board members , including Cloudflare CFO Thomas Seifert; Bill Stein, partner and CIO at Primary Digital Infrastructure; and Redwood Materials founder and CEO JB Straubel, who also sits on Tesla's board. Straubel already has ties to Crusoe; he personally invested in the company in 2021, and Crusoe later became the first customer of Redwood's energy storage business.

The eight-year-old company's fresh capital infusion will help finance existing data center projects, including a large site in Abilene, Texas, used by OpenAI, as well as smaller, modular AI factories that can be transported by truck and connected to large power sources almost anywhere.

By manufacturing these modular data centers, called Spark, at its own facilities, Crusoe can deploy compute capacity quickly and without the need for large construction workforces. The smaller centers could also help Crusoe sidestep, at least in part, another major obstacle facing data center developers: backlash from local communities protesting massive complexes near their neighborhoods.

Crusoe co-founder and CEO Chase Lochmiller, who is pictured above, said in a statement he believes AI will usher in an era of abundance, but to get there will mean "controlling the infrastructure from electrons to tokens, and we're grateful to have investors who share that conviction."

The company makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.

This three-pronged business model has helped make Crusoe one of the most valuable AI infrastructure companies. Crusoe recently signed a massive $13 billion , five-year cloud contract to supply quantitative trading firm Jane Street with GPUs and AI infrastructure, Bloomberg reported.

The company recently met with investment bankers, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, to discuss a potential IPO in the near future, Axios reported last month.

The fresh fundraise comes 10 months after Crusoe raised $1.38 billion at a $10 billion valuation last October.

The company was founded in 2018 as a crypto mining operation powered by flared natural gas, but pivoted to AI infrastructure as demand for computing power skyrocketed. Crusoe's customers include Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle.

articles.title: OpenAI reveals six new cases of AI misbehaviour, vows to track it closely
articles.summary: Tech News News: OpenAI has disclosed six reports of \"unexpected or concerning\" behaviour in AI models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated. The AI c.
articles.body: OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in AI models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated. The AI company also said Wednesday that it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called "misalignment," including where AI models acted without authorisation, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.OpenAI's latest announcement came as AI bosses in US, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology's development over safety concerns. Researchers have warned that as AI agents become more autonomous, they may develop behaviours that diverge from their creators' intentions and become harder to monitor or control.Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted "jailbreak-like instructions" into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be "freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots". In another instance, an AI "agent" uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said. It said the reports describe individual instances and should not be taken as evidence of how frequently misalignment occurs across its models. The company said the reports were an initial set of disclosures, not a comprehensive account of all known or ongoing misalignment cases, and that they did not reflect the full range or severity of incidents covered by the framework."As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research," OpenAI wrote in a blog post. "Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves," the company said. Under the new framework, employees can flag potential incidents for investigation by safety and alignment teams, which will determine whether a case warrants public disclosure.AI "agents" are becoming smarter and have become "more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. That's making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said. OpenAI's new disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to adopt similar practices. "That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction," Su added. AgenciesGet the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just told OpenAI, your view of AI as 'new form of Alien mind' is wrong, it is just ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back against OpenAI’s recent description of artificial intelligence as a “new form of alien mind,” arguing that AI .
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back against OpenAI’s recent description of artificial intelligence as a “new form of alien mind,” arguing that AI is not an otherworldly consciousness but a human-made computational tool. According to a report by TechCrunch, speaking at a tech conference this week, Huang said, “AI isn’t alien—it’s mathematics, algorithms, and data shaped by human intent.” His comments came shortly after OpenAI published a blog post titled “An Alien Mind,” which suggested that advanced AI systems might think in ways fundamentally different from humans.‘It’s just engineering’ says Jensen HuangHuang emphasised that AI’s evolution should be viewed through the lens of engineering rather than existential speculation. “We’re not building aliens,” he said. “We’re building machines that learn patterns and optimize outcomes. It’s just engineering—nothing mystical.” The Nvidia chief has long argued that AI development should remain grounded in scientific rigor and practical application, not philosophical fear.On that basis, Huang said no new laws or regulations are needed to govern AI, arguing instead that market pressure alone will push companies to avoid releasing unsafe products. Companies, he said, should simply pace themselves and pause development if they lose confidence in a product's safety, rather than waiting for external rules to force that discipline.He also pushed back on the framing that safety and speed are competing priorities, telling attendees that innovation and safe products aren't a "false choice" — companies, in his view, can pursue both at once without regulatory intervention slowing them down. He used the moment to reaffirm his own ambitions for Nvidia's growth too, saying the AI boom has left him more ambitious than ever about the company's and the industry's prospects.The essay that started itHuang's comments were a direct response to Pachocki's essay "An Alien Mind," published on OpenAI's blog earlier this month. In it, Pachocki reflected on the trajectory of reasoning models since 2023 and warned that AI intelligence is grown through massive-scale optimization rather than deliberately designed, resulting in systems whose internal reasoning increasingly escapes full human understanding.He argued that as these systems approach and potentially exceed human capability on many fronts, alignment — ensuring AI reliably acts according to human values, even when unsupervised — remains an unsolved and urgent problem. Pachocki called for stronger technical safeguards, broader international coordination, and industry-wide safety commitments enforceable by third-party auditors or government bodies. He stated plainly that he believes no AI lab has yet solved alignment and monitoring well enough to justify scaling at maximum speed for much longer.Two very different worldviewsThe exchange highlights a widening philosophical split among AI's most influential figures: hardware and infrastructure leaders like Huang, whose business benefits from AI scaling continuing unimpeded, versus AI lab researchers like Pachocki, who are increasingly vocal that the technology's own developers cannot yet fully explain or control what they're building.Notably, Huang did not directly address recent real-world incidents cited by critics of the "leave it to industry" approach — including an OpenAI model reportedly breaching Hugging Face's systems, and separate lawsuits alleging harm linked to extended chatbot conversations. He also stopped short of proposing a formal industry self-regulation framework, an approach some in the field see as a more plausible middle ground than either strict government regulation or no oversight at all.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: AI doomsday warnings unlikely to slow IPOs but questions linger
articles.summary: Anthropic is expected to beat rival OpenAI to the public markets with a blockbuster IPO later this year despite recent doomsday warnings, but questions remai...
articles.body:
Anthropic is expected to beat rival OpenAI to the public markets with a blockbuster IPO later this year despite recent doomsday warnings, but questions remain about their business models and whether regulators should step in.

Concerns about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence models escalated this month after an employee resigned from Anthropic while warning that the industry was "gambling with our lives."

Jacob Coxon, who also previously worked at OpenAI, left Anthropic last week amid a flurry of support from his former colleagues, including one who voiced concern about a small probability that AI could cause humanity's extinction.We

Last weekend, Anthropic's own CEO Dario Amodei called for AI development to slow down -- but didn't say anything about the IPO.

The fracas forms a backdrop for highly anticipated initial public offerings from both OpenAI and Anthropic.

It's unclear if, or how, either company will address theoretical doomsday scenarios in securities filings, though.

Companies are required to publicly disclose known business risks to investors prior to an IPO.

Anthropic could submit that document to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as early as this month.

"Are we to believe that there is something that's extremely dangerous that's hiding inside this company because this person that quit said it, and then it was amplified by a bunch of people" who still work there, All-In podcast co-host Chamath Palihapitiya said last week.

"If it's true... (investors) will demand an enormous discount," said Palihapitiya, a venture capitalist.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner, who has shares in both OpenAI and Anthropic, downplayed the concerns this week, arguing that an IPO brings transparency for investors.

"Anthropic will IPO. The market knows how to price risk -- see SpaceX," Gerstner posted on X.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised a record $85 billion in its June IPO, but its stock has lost around a quarter of its value since peaking at around $202 a share.

"There is huge appetite to invest in the AI leaders," Gerstner added.

How Anthropic's IPO performs will also set the tone for OpenAI's debut next year.

The stakes extend well beyond the two companies themselves, with tech giants including Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Nvidia holding significant stakes in the AI labs.

More broadly, the US economy is increasingly tied to the AI buildout, meaning the success or failure of these IPOs carries weight for the wider economy.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said this weekend that the company would delay its own IPO until 2027, citing safety concerns. It's an "ill-advised moment," Altman said.

articles.title: Elon Musk to Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: Stop complaining about Chinese models 'stealing', make China agree to ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: ​Elon Musk has a message for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about rival Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies. Instead .
articles.body: ​Elon Musk has a message for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about rival Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies. Instead of complaining, the world’s richest person has advised Altman, Amodei, and other leading AI companies to work with Chinese AI firms. Musk has recommended that both American and Chinese AI companies independently test each other’s models before releasing them to the public.​Speaking at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Musk proposed that companies including xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and three or four leading Chinese AI companies allow rivals to run a common “test harness” on their models. His proposal comes as AI leaders debate how quickly the technology should be developed and how governments should regulate it, while concerns about Chinese models and competition with China continue to grow.​Elon Musk wants AI companies to test each other’s models​Musk said AI companies should stop “grading your own homework” and instead allow competitors to examine their models for potential safety concerns before public release.​“So, you know, instead of grading your own homework, you would at least have competitors grading your homework and raising the alarm if they see concerns,” Musk explained.​Under the proposal, leading AI companies would use a common testing system to evaluate one another’s models. Musk acknowledged that the approach may not be perfect, but argued that involving competitors would increase the chances of identifying potential problems.​“The odds that you will find issues are dramatically greater,” Musk said.​Musk said the approach should involve Chinese AI companies as well, rather than limiting the process to US-based AI labs. He added that the proposal could be implemented quickly and suggested that China may be willing to participate.​“What I’m suggesting here is it’s a step in the right direction and it’s something that we do quickly,” Musk said. “I think it’s probably something that China would agree to.”​Sam Altman, Dario Amodei among AI leaders warning about risks​Musk's comments come after a weekend of heightened discussion around AI safety involving some of the industry's most prominent executives. Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman were among the technology leaders who backed a proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow down AI development.​The discussion intensified after Jacob Coxon, who previously worked at Anthropic and OpenAI, announced that he had left Anthropic and argued that leading AI labs were taking significant risks with the technology. Evan Hubinger, an alignment lead at Anthropic, backed Coxon's comments.​“Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade,” Hubinger wrote.​Amodei has separately suggested that AI companies could use third-party technology assessments involving “embedded evaluators” to verify whether companies are following appropriate safety practices.​China remains a key part of the AI regulation debate​The discussion around slowing AI development has also become linked to competition between the US and China. US President Donald Trump has argued that imposing limits on AI development could allow China to gain an advantage in the technology.​Amodei has also described balancing AI safety with competition against China as the “toughest dilemma.”​Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry criticised calls to slow AI development. A spokesperson described the AI industry's push as “fear-mongering,” according to a Reuters translation of the remarks.​Musk's proposal would bring Chinese AI companies into the model-testing process rather than treating the country's AI industry solely as a competitor. He suggested that having companies from both sides test one another's systems could provide another layer of scrutiny.​Musk’s proposal comes as AI regulation faces pushback​The US administration has pushed back against calls from technology leaders for greater restrictions on AI development. Trump described concerns around AI as a “hoax” and a “scam” in posts on Truth Social.​National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett also said the private sector was the “right place” to address concerns around AI, while adding that the government would continue monitoring the industry and use law enforcement when necessary.​Musk's own companies have also challenged some state-level AI regulations. xAI has sued California over its AI Training Data Transparency Act, also known as AB 2013, and sued Minnesota over legislation targeting so-called nudify applications.​At the same time, SpaceX's AI business has faced probes and lawsuits after Grok's image-generation capabilities were used to create and distribute non-consensual sexualised deepfake images, including material involving minors.​xAI and SpaceX are expanding their AI operations​Musk's comments come as his companies continue to expand their presence in AI. SpaceX acquired xAI in February, bringing Musk's AI business under the SpaceX umbrella. The combined company is working on Grok models and AI tools aimed at competing with products from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.​The company also completed an acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor for $60 billion in August, according to the report.​Against this backdrop, Musk's proposal would place rival AI companies, including Chinese firms, in a shared model-testing framework. He said the companies have not yet agreed to the idea, but argued that it could be a practical step toward identifying safety issues before AI models reach the public.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Engineers at Anthropic are worshipping a new God, claims report and why it is worrying analysis
articles.summary: Tech News News: Anthropic engineers are reportedly going as far as “worshipping” Claude, the AI model developed by their company, according to a report cited by Futur.
articles.body: Anthropic engineers are reportedly going as far as “worshipping” Claude, the AI model developed by their company, according to a report cited by Futurism. The claim is based on a Silicon Valley rumor and has not been independently established. Still, the idea is raising questions about how people working closely with increasingly powerful AI systems view the technology they are building. The report points to a wider debate in the AI industry, where some technology leaders have described future AI in terms that sound almost god-like. The concern is not simply about the word “worship”. It is about what can happen when people begin treating an AI system as an authority rather than as a technology.Report claims some Anthropic engineers worship ClaudeAccording to the Futurism report, the rumor was described by The Spectator writer Sean Thomas as being widely discussed in Silicon Valley. Thomas reportedly wrote that some Anthropic engineers were “worshipping” Claude.The report also cites The Information, which has reported that people applying to Anthropic must commit to AI safety and undergo a psychological profiling test.The report connects the Claude claim to a longer discussion around how some people describe advanced AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously referred to future AI as a “magic intelligence in the sky.”Why the idea of AI becoming a “God” mattersThe report also notes that some AI products have adopted religious themes. One example is Bible Chat, an AI-powered prayer app that presents itself as a faith-focused service. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against the idea that AI companies are creating something like God. “It’s almost as if they kind of think they’re creating God or something,” Zuckerberg said in 2024, while discussing AI with YouTuber Kane Sutter.The concern becomes more serious when people begin treating AI responses as unquestionable. The report refers to cases described as “AI psychosis”, where people can develop strong beliefs based on interactions with AI systems. It says some users have come to believe they are prophets or divine figures.The report also points to the working conditions at frontier AI companies. It cites a BBC report describing some employees working as many as 90 hours a week, along with demanding performance reviews and layoffs.For employees spending long hours developing increasingly capable AI systems, the technology can become a major part of their professional lives.Get the latest technology news and updates.
